4848-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Parma's river campaigns of 1586 form the backbone of this volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the fighting along the Meuse, Waal, and Rhine. Fortified towns decide who controls the countryside, so Parma besieges Grave, takes the Meuse, and later storms Neusz, whose garrison meets a grim fate.

Leicester celebrates at Utrecht, rages at Grave's surrender, and takes the field himself, reducing Doesburg and besieging Zutphen. The campaign ends with the wounding and death of Sir Philip Sidney after the battle of Warnsfeld. Motley mixes siege detail with character, showing how river towns and proud commanders shaped a war.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1586c:
John Lothrop Motley's ninth chapter, in this portion of his History of the United Netherlands, turns to military plans for 1586. The scene shifts to the debatable country on the Batavian border. The archiepiscopal electorate of Cologne lies desolate along the dividing Rhine. Cologne, Neusz, and Rheinberg stand endangered on the river.

The Elector's war drags Spanish and Dutch forces into Germany's quarrels. Towns in Westphalia are invaded, ravaged, and plundered around the unfortunate district. Motley shows how the Netherlands war overflowed its banks, like the rivers of his landscape. Every army lived on the country, and every country suffered alike. This slice of the history widens the reader's map: the revolt of the Netherlands was also a German and European war. Strategy here is mostly geography, rivers, and starving garrisons.
uslaw-usc-t2-s136c:
Section 136c of Title 2 of the United States Code widens what the Library of Congress may buy with its salary money. Appropriations acts give the Library funds for salaries, a narrow label. From October 1, 1983, this section stretches the label to cover three needs.

First, the salary funds may pay for personnel security and suitability investigations of Library employees. Screening the people who guard the nation's collections is charged to the same account as their pay. Second, the funds cover special and temporary services. Workers engaged by the day or hour, or in piecework, fall in this class. Third, services may be bought as authorized by section 3109 of Title 5, the expert and consultant provision. The section is a quiet flexibility clause in the Library's housekeeping law.
